facts.fact_text: The applicant organisation is a non-governmental human rights organisation.
The applicant organisation is based in Yerevan.
On 12 May 2007, a third person identified as L.G. died while at a police station.
The death of L.G. on 12 May 2007 provoked an outcry among Armenian human rights groups and civil society.
On 6 May 2008, the applicant organisation applied to the Mayor of Yerevan, notifying its intention to hold a mourning march on the first anniversary of L.G.'s death.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to take place on 12 May 2008.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to take place from 8 p.m. to 9.30 p.m.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to start at Republic Square in Yerevan.
The mourning march notified by the applicant organisation was planned to continue through Nalbandyan Street in the direction of the police station.
On 8 May 2008, the Mayor of Yerevan decided to ban the planned mourning march.
On 12 May 2008, the police prevented the organisers from holding the planned mourning march.
The police who prevented the organisers from holding the planned mourning march on 12 May 2008 had apparently been informed of the Mayor of Yerevan's ban decision of 8 May 2008.
The Mayor of Yerevan's decision to ban the planned mourning march was made with reference to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.
The Mayor of Yerevan's decision to ban the planned mourning march was made with reference to Section 13 § 1 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it is aimed at forcibly overthrowing the constitutional order.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it is aimed at inflaming ethnic, racial or religious hatred.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it is aimed at campaigning for violence or war.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it may lead to mass disorder and crime.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it may lead to undermining national security, public order and the health and morality of society.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority may ban the holding of a public event if, according to credible data, it may lead to encroachments on the constitutional rights and freedoms of others.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, data may be considered credible if the Police or the National Security Service under the Government of Armenia have issued an official opinion on the data.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the Police or the National Security Service under the Government of Armenia shall also issue an opinion if the grounds for banning cease to exist.

According to Section 9 § 4 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, an official opinion from the Police or the National Security Service under the Government of Armenia is also issued in cases envisaged by Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, in cases where mass public events have turned into mass disorder resulting in human casualties, the competent authority may temporarily ban the holding of mass public events in order to prevent new crimes.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the temporary ban on mass public events may be imposed only given that other means of prevention have been exhausted.

According to Section 9 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the temporary ban on mass public events shall last until the circumstances of the crime and the identity of the offenders have been disclosed.
According to Section 10 § 1 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, mass public events may be held only after notifying the competent authority in writing.

According to Section 10 § 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the organisers shall send written notification of the intention to hold a mass public event to the head of the local authority where the event is to be organised.
According to Section 10 § 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, if the public event is to be held in Yerevan, the written notification shall be sent to the Mayor of Yerevan.
According to Section 10 § 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the written notification shall be sent not later than five working days before the planned date of the event.
According to Section 10 § 4 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the written notification shall be sent not earlier than twenty days before the planned date of the event.
According to Section 12 § 1 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority shall examine the notification within 72 hours of receipt.
According to Section 12 § 1 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, notifications shall be examined in the order in which they have been received.

According to Section 12 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, in the absence of the circumstances mentioned in Section 13 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the notification of the mass public event shall be taken into consideration and the event shall be held in the place and at the time indicated in the notification.

According to Section 12 § 6 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, in the presence of the circumstances mentioned in Section 13 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, a decision shall be taken banning the mass public event.

According to Section 12 § 7 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority shall immediately inform the organisers of its decision taken as a result of examination of the notification.

According to Section 12 § 7 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority shall immediately inform the police of its decision taken as a result of examination of the notification.

According to Section 12 § 7 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the competent authority shall post up its decision on its premises in a specially designated spot, accessible and visible to the public.

According to Section 12 § 7 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the decision of the competent authority shall remain posted up until 6 p.m. on the planned date of the mass public event indicated in the notification.

According to Section 12 § 8 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, should the competent authority not take a decision banning the mass public event, the organisers shall have the right to hold the mass public event on the terms and conditions set forth in the notification.

According to Section 13 § 1 (3) of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, a mass public event may be banned only when, inter alia, there exist grounds stipulated by Section 9 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act.

According to Section 13 § 2 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, a decision banning a mass public event shall contain a reasoned and clear explanation of the grounds on which the mass public event is banned.
According to Section 13 § 3 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, a decision banning a mass public event may be contested before the courts.
According to Section 13 § 3 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, the court shall adopt a judgment within 24 hours of a challenge to a ban decision.

According to Section 13 § 3 of the Assemblies, Rallies, Marches and Demonstrations Act, a court judgment annulling a decision banning a mass public event shall enter into force from the moment of its delivery.
According to Articles 66-69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, four types of application may be lodged with the Administrative Court.

According to Article 66 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to challenge may be lodged with the Administrative Court, seeking the annulment in part or in whole of the administrative act constituting an interference.
According to Article 67 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to oblige may be lodged with the Administrative Court, seeking the adoption of a favourable administrative act.

According to Article 68 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to perform an action may be lodged with the Administrative Court, seeking the performance of certain actions or refraining from certain actions.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to recognise may be lodged with the Administrative Court, seeking the recognition of existence or absence of a legal relationship.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to recognise may be lodged only if it is impossible to lodge an application under Articles 66-68 of the Code of Administrative Procedure.
According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to recognise may seek to recognise the invalidity of an administrative act.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, an application to recognise may seek to recognise the unlawfulness of an interfering administrative act which is no longer in force, or of actions or inaction, if the applicant has a justified interest in doing so.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, a justified interest in recognising the unlawfulness of an administrative act exists if there is a risk of adoption of a similar act or of performance of similar actions or inaction.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, a justified interest in recognising the unlawfulness of an administrative act exists if the applicant intends to claim pecuniary damage.

According to Article 69 of the Code of Administrative Procedure, a justified interest in recognising the unlawfulness of an administrative act exists if the applicant seeks to restore his honour, dignity or reputation.
